    graph = defaultdict(list)

Consistent Hashing
Problem with naive modulo hashing: adding/removing 1 server remaps N/S keys (massive cache miss storm).

Ring approach: Hash servers and keys to same circular space (0 to 2^32). A key is assigned to the first server found clockwise from its hash position.
Virtual Nodes
Each physical server = 100-200 virtual nodes on the ring → even distribution even with few servers. Fewer hot spots. When server added/removed: only 1/N keys remapped.
class ConsistentHash:
    def __init__(self, replicas=150):
        self.ring = {}
        self.sorted_keys = []
        self.replicas = replicas

    def add_server(self, server):
        for i in range(self.replicas):
            key = hash(f'{server}:{i}')
            self.ring[key] = server
        self.sorted_keys = sorted(self.ring)

    def get_server(self, item):
        h = hash(item)
        for k in self.sorted_keys:
            if h <= k: return self.ring[k]
        return self.ring[self.sorted_keys[0]]  # wrap around

Strong Consistency
All nodes see the same data at the same time. After a write completes, all reads return the new value. Requires synchronous replication. Used in: financial systems, leader election (etcd, ZooKeeper).

Processes vs Threads
  • Process: Independent address space, separate heap/stack/code/data. Isolated — one process crash doesn't affect others. IPC needed (pipes, sockets, shared memory).

  • Process switch: save/restore full CPU state + page table switch (TLB flush) → ~100μs
  • Thread switch (same process): save/restore registers, stack pointer. No TLB flush → ~1-10μs
  • Goroutine/fiber switch: userspace, ~100ns

Scheduling Algorithms

  • SJF: Shortest job first. Optimal average wait time. Requires knowing burst time.

Coffman Conditions for Deadlock
ALL 4 must hold simultaneously for deadlock:
  • Mutual Exclusion: Resource can only be held by one process
  • Hold and Wait: Process holds resources while waiting for more
  • No Preemption: Resources can't be forcibly taken away
  • Circular Wait: Chain of processes each waiting for next in chain
Prevention Strategies
  • Break Hold and Wait: request all resources at once (but reduces concurrency)
  • Break Circular Wait: impose total ordering on lock acquisition (always lock A before B)
  • Allow Preemption: rollback and retry (used in databases)
  • Detection + Recovery: build wait-for graph, detect cycles, kill one process
Banker's Algorithm
Safe state check: simulate allocation, see if all processes can eventually complete. Grant request only if system remains in safe state. O(n²×m) too slow for real OS but used in theory.

On fork(), parent and child share the same physical pages. Pages are marked read-only. On first write by either process → page fault → kernel copies the page → each gets their own copy. Non-written pages are shared forever.

TCP Handshake
Client          Server
  |---SYN(seq=x)---->|  Client: CLOSED→SYN_SENT
  |<--SYN-ACK(seq=y,ack=x+1)---|
  |---ACK(ack=y+1)-->|  Both: ESTABLISHED

Teardown (4-way):

  |<--ACK-----------|
  |<--FIN-----------|

Compare-And-Swap (CAS)
Atomic hardware instruction: CAS(addr, expected, new) → bool. If *addr == expected, atomically set *addr = new and return true. Else return false.
Lock-free Stack with CAS
class LockFreeStack<T> {
    AtomicReference<Node<T>> top = new AtomicReference<>();
    
    void push(T val) {
        Node<T> newNode = new Node<>(val);
        do {
            newNode.next = top.get();  // read current top
        } while (!top.compareAndSet(newNode.next, newNode));  // retry if top changed
    }
    
    T pop() {
        Node<T> old;
        do {
            old = top.get();
            if (old == null) return null;
        } while (!top.compareAndSet(old, old.next));
        return old.val;
    }
}
CAS vs Mutex
CAS: no sleep, no context switch, no kernel call. But: retry loop wastes CPU under high contention. Best for: low contention, short operations. Use mutex for long critical sections.

class TokenBucketRateLimiter {
    private final long capacity;
    private final double refillRatePerMs;
    private double tokens;
    private long lastRefillTime;

    public TokenBucketRateLimiter(long capacity, long refillPerSecond) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.refillRatePerMs = refillPerSecond / 1000.0;
        this.tokens = capacity;
        this.lastRefillTime = System.currentTimeMillis();
    }

    public synchronized boolean allowRequest() {
        refill();
        if (tokens >= 1) { tokens--; return true; }
        return false;
    }

    private void refill() {
        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        double toAdd = (now - lastRefillTime) * refillRatePerMs;
        tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + toAdd);
        lastRefillTime = now;
    }
}

class KVStore {
    TreeMap<String,String> memTable = new TreeMap<>();
    List<SSTable> ssTables = new ArrayList<>();
    WriteAheadLog wal;
    final int MEM_TABLE_LIMIT = 1_000_000;

    synchronized void put(String key, String value) {
        wal.append(key, value);
        memTable.put(key, value);
        if (memTable.size() >= MEM_TABLE_LIMIT) flush();
    }

    String get(String key) {
        if (memTable.containsKey(key)) return memTable.get(key);
        for (int i = ssTables.size()-1; i >= 0; i--) {
            if (ssTables.get(i).bloomFilter.mightContain(key))
                return ssTables.get(i).get(key);  // binary search in sorted file
        }
        return null;
    }
}

class ConnectionPool {
    BlockingDeque<Connection> pool;
    AtomicInteger totalCreated;
    int maxSize, minIdle;
    long acquireTimeoutMs;

    Connection borrow() throws Exception {
        Connection conn = pool.pollFirst(acquireTimeoutMs, MILLISECONDS);
        if (conn == null) {
            if (totalCreated.get() < maxSize) {
                conn = createConnection(); totalCreated.incrementAndGet();
            } else throw new TimeoutException("Pool exhausted");
        }
        if (!conn.isValid()) { conn.close(); return borrow(); }  // retry
        return conn;
    }

    void release(Connection conn) {
        if (conn.isValid()) pool.offerFirst(conn);
        else { conn.close(); totalCreated.decrementAndGet(); }
    }

    // Health check thread: periodically validate idle connections
    void startHealthCheck() {
        scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(() -> {
            pool.forEach(c -> { if (!c.isValid()) { pool.remove(c); totalCreated.decrementAndGet(); } });
            while (pool.size() < minIdle) pool.add(createConnection());
        }, 30, 30, SECONDS);
    }
}

text: Docker container vs Virtual Machine — key differences?

Answer
Virtual Machine: Full OS per VM, hardware emulation via hypervisor (Type-1: bare metal, Type-2: hosted). Heavy: ~GBs, slow boot (~minutes), strong isolation.

text: How do Docker image layers work? (Union filesystem)
answer_hint:
Answer
Docker images are built as read-only layers stacked using a Union Filesystem (OverlayFS/AUFS). Each RUN, COPY, ADD instruction in a Dockerfile creates a new layer.

When a container runs, Docker adds a thin read-write layer on top (Copy-on-Write). Writes go to the container layer; reads search layers bottom-up.
Dockerfile Layer Example
FROM ubuntu:22.04          # Layer 1: base OS
RUN apt-get install -y java # Layer 2: java install
COPY app.jar /app/          # Layer 3: app binary
CMD ["java", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]  # metadata only

  • Order layers from least to most frequently changing
  • Combine RUN commands to reduce layer count
  • Use .dockerignore to exclude build artifacts
  • Use multi-stage builds to discard build-time layers

COPY --from=builder /app/server /server

text: Implement a thread-safe LRU Cache in C++
answer_hint:
Design
std::list (doubly-linked list) + std::unordered_map<K, list::iterator>.
Most recently used at front. On access: move node to front. On eviction: remove from back.
Implementation
template<typename K, typename V>
class LRUCache {
    int cap;
    std::list<std::pair<K,V>> lst;
    std::unordered_map<K, decltype(lst.begin())> mp;
    std::mutex mu;
public:
    LRUCache(int cap) : cap(cap) {}

    std::optional<V> get(const K& key) {
        std::lock_guard lock(mu);
        auto it = mp.find(key);
        if (it == mp.end()) return {};
        lst.splice(lst.begin(), lst, it->second);  // move to front
        return it->second->second;
    }

    void put(const K& key, V val) {
        std::lock_guard lock(mu);
        if (mp.count(key)) lst.erase(mp[key]);
        else if ((int)lst.size() == cap) {
            mp.erase(lst.back().first);
            lst.pop_back();
        }
        lst.push_front({key, val});
        mp[key] = lst.begin();
    }
};
Complexity
get/put: O(1) average. Thread-safe with a single mutex. For higher concurrency: use reader-writer lock or shard by key hash.

text: Implement a lock-free stack using CAS
answer_hint:
Design
Use std::atomic<Node*> for head. CAS in a loop for push/pop.
Implementation
template<typename T>
class LockFreeStack {
    struct Node { T data; Node* next; };
    std::atomic<Node*> head{nullptr};
public:
    void push(T val) {
        Node* n = new Node{std::move(val), nullptr};
        n->next = head.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        while (!head.compare_exchange_weak(n->next, n,
               std::memory_order_release, std::memory_order_relaxed));
    }
    std::optional<T> pop() {
        Node* old = head.load(std::memory_order_acquire);
        while (old && !head.compare_exchange_weak(old, old->next,
               std::memory_order_release, std::memory_order_acquire));
        if (!old) return {};
        T val = std::move(old->data);
        // DANGER: delete old  ← ABA problem / use-after-free with concurrent pops
        return val;
    }
};
ABA Problem
After loading old = A, another thread pops A, pushes B, pushes A back. CAS sees A and succeeds but old->next points to stale node. Fix: tagged pointers (version counter) or hazard pointers for safe memory reclamation.

text: Rule of 0, Rule of 3, Rule of 5 — explain with examples
answer_hint:
Rule of 3 (pre-C++11)
If you define any of: destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, you should define all three. (Managing raw resource → need custom copy + destructor)
Rule of 5 (C++11+)
Add move constructor + move assignment. Without them, moves fall back to copies (expensive).
class Buffer {
    char* data; size_t sz;
public:
    Buffer(size_t n) : data(new char[n]), sz(n) {}
    ~Buffer() { delete[] data; }               // 1: destructor
    Buffer(const Buffer& o)                   // 2: copy ctor
        : data(new char[o.sz]), sz(o.sz) { memcpy(data,o.data,sz); }
    Buffer& operator=(const Buffer& o) {       // 3: copy assign
        if(this==&o) return *this;
        delete[] data; sz=o.sz; data=new char[sz]; memcpy(data,o.data,sz); return *this;
    }
    Buffer(Buffer&& o) noexcept                // 4: move ctor
        : data(o.data), sz(o.sz) { o.data=nullptr; o.sz=0; }
    Buffer& operator=(Buffer&& o) noexcept {   // 5: move assign
        if(this==&o) return *this;
        delete[] data; data=o.data; sz=o.sz; o.data=nullptr; return *this;
    }
};
Rule of 0
Best practice: design classes to own no raw resources. Use RAII wrappers (unique_ptr, vector, string). Then you need ZERO custom special members — compiler generates correct ones.

What is CRTP
Base class templated on its derived class. Enables static polymorphism (compile-time virtual dispatch) — zero vtable overhead.
Example: Static Polymorphism
template<typename Derived>
struct Shape {
    double area() const {
        return static_cast<const Derived*>(this)->area_impl();
    }
};
struct Circle : Shape<Circle> {
    double r;
    double area_impl() const { return 3.14*r*r; }
};
struct Square : Shape<Square> {
    double s;
    double area_impl() const { return s*s; }
};
// Caller (template function, not virtual):
template<typename S> void print(const Shape<S>& s) { std::cout << s.area(); }
CRTP for Mixins
template<typename T>
struct Comparable {
    bool operator!=(const T& o) const { return !(static_cast<const T&>(*this)==o); }
    bool operator> (const T& o) const { return o < static_cast<const T&>(*this); }
    // Derived only implements operator== and operator<
};
struct Point : Comparable<Point> {
    int x,y;
    bool operator==(const Point& o) const { return x==o.x && y==o.y; }
    bool operator< (const Point& o) const { return x<o.x || (x==o.x && y<o.y); }
};
CRTP vs Concepts (C++20)
CRTP: complex syntax, but works pre-C++20 with zero runtime cost. C++20 Concepts: cleaner constraints but still need virtual for runtime polymorphism.

Diamond Problem
struct A { int x; };

struct C : virtual A {};

With virtual inheritance, B and C each store a virtual base pointer (vbptr) pointing to the shared A subobject. D's constructor directly initializes A.

Full Producer-Consumer
#include <mutex>
#include <condition_variable>
#include <queue>

std::mutex mtx;
std::condition_variable cv;
std::queue<int> q;
bool done = false;

void producer() {
    for(int i=0;i<10;i++) {
        std::unique_lock lock(mtx);
        q.push(i);
        cv.notify_one();  // wake one consumer
    }
    { std::lock_guard lock(mtx); done=true; }
    cv.notify_all();
}

void consumer() {
    while(true) {
        std::unique_lock lock(mtx);
        cv.wait(lock, []{ return !q.empty() || done; });  // predicate prevents spurious wakeup
        while(!q.empty()) { process(q.front()); q.pop(); }
        if(done) break;
    }
}
Spurious Wakeups
Always use cv.wait(lock, predicate) — without predicate, spurious wakeups cause bugs. Equivalent to: while(!pred()) cv.wait(lock);

Java platform thread = OS thread. Creating 10,000 threads = 10,000 OS threads. Each uses ~1MB stack. I/O blocking wastes the OS thread.

        if (key.isAcceptable()) { accept(key); }
        else if (key.isReadable()) { read(key); }

}

CountDownLatch
One-time gate. Threads await() until count reaches 0 via countDown(). Cannot be reset.

// Each thread calls barrier.await() — blocked until 3 threads reach barrier

Controls access to N permits. acquire() blocks if 0 permits. release() returns one.
Semaphore sem = new Semaphore(5);  // max 5 concurrent threads
sem.acquire();  // blocks if 5 already running
try { doWork(); } finally { sem.release(); }

phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance() — arrive + wait for next phase.

  • CyclicBarrier: parallel computation phases (map-reduce stages)

answer_hint:
Lazy Evaluation
Intermediate operations (filter, map, flatMap) return a new Stream — nothing executes. Terminal operations (collect, forEach, reduce) trigger the pipeline. Short-circuit ops (findFirst, limit) stop early.
Pipeline Example
List<String> result = list.stream()
    .filter(s -> s.length() > 3)   // lazy: creates filter stage
    .map(String::toUpperCase)         // lazy: creates map stage
    .sorted()                          // stateful: must see all elements!
    .limit(5)                          // short-circuit terminal
    .collect(Collectors.toList());     // triggers whole pipeline
Spliterator

ReadWriteLock rwl = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();

text: Java GC algorithms — Mark-Sweep, Mark-Compact, Copying, Generational
answer_hint:
Mark-Sweep
Mark: traverse GC roots, mark all reachable objects. Sweep: scan heap, free unmarked objects. Problem: fragmentation — free spaces scattered.
Mark-Compact
Mark phase same. Compact phase: slide all live objects to one end. No fragmentation. Slower than sweep (extra copy). G1GC uses this for selected regions.
Copying Collection
Divide heap into From/To spaces. Copy live objects to To, flip spaces. No fragmentation, fast allocation (bump pointer). Wastes 50% of heap. Used for young generation.
Generational Hypothesis
Most objects die young. Java heap split:
  • Young (Eden + 2 Survivors): Minor GC — fast, copying collector
  • Old (Tenured): Major/Full GC — mark-compact or concurrent marking
Promotion: object surviving N minor GCs (default 15) moves to Old gen.
G1GC
Divides heap into equal regions (~1-32MB). Marks concurrently. Selects regions with most garbage (Garbage-First) for collection. Pause target: -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200.

import "golang.org/x/sync/errgroup"

func fetchAll(ctx context.Context, ids []int) ([]User, error) {
    g, ctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)
    results := make([]User, len(ids))

    for i, id := range ids {
        i, id := i, id  // capture loop vars
        g.Go(func() error {
            user, err := fetchUser(ctx, id)
            if err != nil { return err }
            results[i] = user
            return nil

        return nil, fmt.Errorf("fetchAll: %w", err)

    return results, nil

text: Go GMP scheduler — deep dive (G, M, P, work stealing)
answer_hint:
GMP Model
  • G (Goroutine): Lightweight coroutine. ~2KB initial stack, grows dynamically. Millions possible.
  • M (Machine/Thread): OS thread. One M executes one G at a time. Limited by GOMAXPROCS for Go code; more Ms created for blocking syscalls.
  • P (Processor): Scheduling context. GOMAXPROCS Ps (default = CPU cores). Each P has a local run queue (LRQ) of Gs.
Scheduling Flow
1. goroutine created → added to P's LRQ
2. P pops G from LRQ, assigns to M → runs
3. G blocks on syscall → M + G detached from P
   → P finds idle M (or creates new) → continues running other Gs
4. Syscall completes → G goes back to global run queue (GRQ)
5. Work stealing: idle P steals half of busy P's LRQ → balanced load
Preemption
Go uses cooperative preemption (yield at function calls) + async preemption (sysmon thread sends SIGURG after 10ms to interrupt G). Long CPU-bound goroutines preempted automatically.
GOMAXPROCS
Number of OS threads for Go code = number of Ps. runtime.GOMAXPROCS(n) or GOMAXPROCS=n env var.

func merge(cs ...<-chan int) <-chan int {
    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    out := make(chan int)
    output := func(c <-chan int) {
        defer wg.Done()
        for v := range c { out <- v }
    }
    wg.Add(len(cs))
    for _, c := range cs { go output(c) }
    go func() { wg.Wait(); close(out) }()
    return out
}
Done Channel (Cancellation)
func sq(done <-chan struct{}, in <-chan int) <-chan int {
    out := make(chan int)
    go func() {
        defer close(out)
        for n := range in {
            select {
            case out <- n*n:
            case <-done: return  // cancelled
            }
        }
    }()
    return out
}

text: Go memory escape analysis and optimization
answer_hint:
Escape Analysis
Go compiler determines at compile time whether a variable can live on the stack (cheap, GC-free) or must escape to the heap (GC pressure, slower).
go build -gcflags='-m -m' ./... shows escape decisions.
Common Escape Causes
  • Variable address taken and returned: return &x — x escapes
  • Stored in interface: var i interface{} = x — x escapes (if not pointer-sized)
  • Closure captures variable: go func(){ use(x) }() — x may escape
  • Slice/map of large type — backing array on heap
Avoiding Escapes
// Bad: escapes to heap
func newPoint(x,y int) *Point { return &Point{x,y} }

// Good: caller allocates on stack
func initPoint(p *Point, x,y int) { p.X,p.Y = x,y }
var p Point; initPoint(&p, 3, 4)  // stays on stack

// Bad: interface boxing causes escape
func log(msg interface{}) { fmt.Println(msg) }  // allocates
// Good:
func log(msg string) { fmt.Println(msg) }  // no alloc
sync.Pool
Reuse heap-allocated objects across goroutines to reduce GC pressure.
pool := sync.Pool{New: func() any { return &Buffer{} }}

text: B+ Tree index internals — structure, splits, range queries
answer_hint:
Structure
  • Internal nodes: keys only, no data. Fan-out typically 100-200 keys per node.
  • Leaf nodes: keys + actual row pointers (or clustered data). Linked list for range scans.
  • Height: ~3-4 levels for millions of rows (log_200(1M) ≈ 3). Fits in memory.
Why B+ over B-Tree
All data in leaves → range queries traverse leaf linked list without backtracking. Internal nodes store more keys (no data) → wider fan-out → shallower tree.
Operations
  • Search: O(log_t n) — traverse from root to leaf
  • Insert: find leaf, insert, split if overflow (cascade up)
  • Delete: find leaf, remove, merge or redistribute if underflow
  • Range scan: find start leaf, traverse linked list → sequential I/O (fast)
Clustered vs Secondary
Clustered: Data rows stored in leaf nodes in index order (InnoDB primary key). One per table.
Secondary: Leaf stores PK value → extra lookup for row data. Multiple allowed.

text: PostgreSQL MVCC — how it achieves non-blocking reads
answer_hint:
MVCC = Multi-Version Concurrency Control
Each row has hidden columns:
  • xmin: transaction ID that inserted this version
  • xmax: transaction ID that deleted/updated this version (0 = still live)
Reads see a snapshot: only versions where xmin ≤ snapshot_xid < xmax.
How it works
T1 (xid=100): UPDATE users SET name='Bob' WHERE id=1
→ Old row: xmin=50, xmax=100  (now dead to T1)
→ New row: xmin=100, xmax=0   (live)

T2 (xid=99, started before T1):
→ Sees old row (xmin=50 <= 99 < xmax=100) ✓
→ Sees 'Alice' — no blocking!

T3 (xid=101, started after T1 commits):
→ Old row: xmax=100 <= 101 → dead, skip
→ New row: xmin=100 <= 101, xmax=0 → live, sees 'Bob' ✓
VACUUM
Dead rows (old versions) accumulate. VACUUM reclaims space. AUTOVACUUM runs automatically. Transaction ID wraparound prevented by freezing old rows.

text: EXPLAIN ANALYZE — reading query execution plans
answer_hint:
Key Operations
  • Seq Scan: Full table scan. Fast for small tables / low selectivity.
  • Index Scan: Uses B+ tree index. Best for high selectivity (<10% rows).
  • Index Only Scan: All needed columns in index (covering index). Fastest.
  • Bitmap Heap Scan: Index scan → bitmap of pages → sorted page access. Good for 5-20% rows.
  • Nested Loop: Join — for each outer row, find matching inner. Good for small outer result.
  • Hash Join: Build hash table from smaller table → probe with larger. Good for large unsorted.
  • Merge Join: Both sides sorted. Fast but needs sort step.
Reading EXPLAIN
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;

-> Index Scan using idx_orders_user on orders
   Index Cond: (user_id = 42)
   rows=150 (estimated)  rows=143 (actual)
   Buffers: shared hit=12  (pages from cache)
   Planning: 0.3ms  Execution: 2.1ms
Tuning Signals
  • Seq scan on large table with high selectivity → missing index
  • Estimated rows ≫ actual → stale statistics → run ANALYZE
  • Sort in plan → add index with ORDER BY columns
  • Hash join with large table → may need work_mem increase

Range Partitioning
Divide by value range. Common for time-series data.
CREATE TABLE orders (id bigint, created_at date, ...)
PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

    FOR VALUES FROM ('2023-01-01') TO ('2024-01-01');

    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2025-01-01');

Distribute evenly by hash of key. Good for write distribution.
PARTITION BY HASH (user_id);
-- Partition 0: user_id % 4 = 0
-- Partition 1: user_id % 4 = 1 ...
List Partitioning
By enumerated values. Good for geographic/categorical data.
PARTITION BY LIST (region);
-- India: ('IN'), US: ('US','CA')
Benefits

  • Faster VACUUM, index maintenance (smaller partitions)

answer_hint:
Replication Mechanics (MySQL binlog / PostgreSQL WAL)
Primary records every write as binary log events. Replica connects, streams binlog, applies changes. Replication can be:
  • Async (default): Primary doesn't wait for replica. Replica may lag.
  • Semi-sync: Primary waits for at least 1 replica to acknowledge before committing.
  • Sync (PostgreSQL synchronous_commit=on): All replicas acknowledge. Highest durability, slowest.
Replication Lag Causes
  • Large transactions (long to replay)
  • High write throughput on primary
  • Network latency between primary and replica
  • Single-threaded replay (older MySQL — use parallel replication)
Handling Lag in Applications
  • Read-your-own-writes: route reads after writes to primary for 1s, or use session stickiness
  • For stale-tolerant reads (reports, analytics): use replica
  • Monitor lag: SHOW REPLICA STATUS → Seconds_Behind_Source

What is a Deadlock
Two or more transactions each hold a lock the other needs.
T1: LOCK A → wait for B
T2: LOCK B → wait for A
→ Circular wait = deadlock
Deadlock Detection
Most DBs run a background detector (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB).
Builds a wait-for graph: node = transaction, edge = T1 waits for lock held by T2. Cycle = deadlock → kill victim transaction (least expensive to rollback).
Prevention Strategies
  • Lock ordering: Always acquire locks in the same global order (e.g., lower ID first)
  • Timeout: SET lock_timeout = '1s' — transaction aborts if wait too long
  • SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED: Skip locked rows instead of waiting (job queues)
  • Reduce transaction scope: Short transactions hold locks briefly
Application-Level Fix
-- Instead of long transaction:
BEGIN;
  UPDATE account SET bal = bal - 100 WHERE id = 1;  -- locks row
  -- ... complex computation (seconds) ...
  UPDATE account SET bal = bal + 100 WHERE id = 2;  -- deadlock risk!
COMMIT;

-- Better: do computation outside transaction, then short UPDATE

text: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) — how databases ensure durability
answer_hint:
What is WAL
Before modifying data pages in memory (buffer pool), the change is written to the WAL log first. On crash: replay WAL from last checkpoint to recover committed transactions. Guarantee: committed data never lost, even on sudden crash.
Write Flow
1. Transaction modifies data in buffer pool (in-memory dirty page)
2. WAL record written to WAL buffer → flushed to disk (fsync)
   [WAL written BEFORE data page written — Write-Ahead!]
3. Transaction commits: commit WAL record flushed
4. Background: dirty pages periodically checkpointed to data files
5. WAL records before checkpoint can be deleted
PostgreSQL WAL
WAL files in pg_wal/. Controls: fsync=on (durability), synchronous_commit=on/off. Turning off synchronous_commit: ~10% faster writes, risk of last 100ms of data on crash.
Uses beyond recovery
  • Streaming replication: replicas stream WAL from primary
  • Point-in-time recovery (PITR): replay WAL to any past state
  • Logical replication: parse WAL for row-level changes (Debezium/CDC)

Why Pool Connections
PostgreSQL creates a new OS process per connection (~5-10MB RAM). Opening connection takes ~30-100ms. 1000 connections = 5-10GB RAM, GC overhead, scheduler pressure.
PgBouncer
Lightweight connection pooler for PostgreSQL. Sits between app and DB.
  • Session mode: App gets same DB connection for session duration. All features work.
  • Transaction mode: Connection returned to pool after each transaction. Supports many more app connections (1000s) with few DB connections (50). Restrictions: no SET, no prepared statements per session.
  • Statement mode: Return after each statement. Most restrictive.

Fast JDBC connection pool.

cfg.setJdbcUrl("jdbc:postgresql://host/db");
cfg.setMaximumPoolSize(10);
cfg.setConnectionTimeout(30000);
cfg.setIdleTimeout(600000);
cfg.setMaxLifetime(1800000);  // 30min to prevent stale conns
DataSource ds = new HikariDataSource(cfg);

Pool size = (core_count × 2) + effective_spindle_count. Smaller than you think — more connections ≠ more throughput.

text: Eventual consistency models — BASE, read-your-writes, monotonic reads
answer_hint:
CAP Theorem Recap
In presence of network partition (P), choose between Consistency (C) or Availability (A). Most distributed systems choose AP → eventual consistency.
BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent)
Contrast to ACID.
  • Basically Available: System works, even during partial failure (stale data OK)
  • Soft State: State may change without input (replication catching up)
  • Eventually Consistent: Given no new updates, all replicas converge to same state
Consistency Models (weakest to strongest)
  • Eventual: Converges eventually. DNS, S3.
  • Monotonic Read: Once you read version V, you never see older version. (client stickiness)
  • Read-Your-Writes: You always see your own writes immediately. (session token pinning)
  • Causal: If A caused B, everyone sees A before B. (vector clocks)
  • Sequential: All operations appear in a global order consistent with program order.
  • Linearizable (Strict): Strongest. Operations appear instantaneous. ZooKeeper, etcd.

TimescaleDB
PostgreSQL extension. Adds hypertables — automatically partitioned by time. Transparent to SQL. Best for: SQL queries + time-series. Compression: 90%+ space savings with native compression.

-- Best index: (a, b, c) — leftmost prefix rule
-- a → equality filter (most selective first)
-- b → range filter
-- c → ORDER BY (eliminates sort)

-- If index is (user_id, email): Index Only Scan — never touches table!
CREATE INDEX idx_user_email ON users(user_id) INCLUDE (email);  -- PostgreSQL

3-Way Handshake (Connection Setup)
Client ----- SYN (seq=x) --------> Server
Client <---- SYN-ACK (seq=y,ack=x+1)- Server
Client ----- ACK (ack=y+1) -------> Server
[Connection ESTABLISHED]

SYN_SENT → SYN_RECEIVED → ESTABLISHED

Active  <-- ACK --- Passive   (ACTIVE: FIN_WAIT_2)

Active  --- ACK --> Passive   (ACTIVE: TIME_WAIT → CLOSED after 2×MSL)

text: TCP flow control (receive window) vs congestion control (CWND)
answer_hint:
Flow Control (Receiver-side)
Prevents sender from overwhelming receiver's buffer.
Receiver advertises receive window (rwnd) in ACK headers. Sender must not have more than rwnd unacknowledged bytes in flight.
Congestion Control (Network-side)
Prevents sender from overwhelming the network (routers/links).
Sender maintains congestion window (cwnd). Effective window = min(cwnd, rwnd).
Congestion Control Phases
  • Slow Start: cwnd=1 MSS → doubles each RTT until ssthresh or packet loss
  • Congestion Avoidance: cwnd grows +1 MSS per RTT (linear)
  • Fast Retransmit: 3 duplicate ACKs → retransmit lost segment immediately (don't wait for timeout)
  • Fast Recovery (CUBIC, BBR): On loss: ssthresh = cwnd/2, cwnd = ssthresh (not back to 1)
BBR (Google)
Model-based congestion control. Estimates bottleneck bandwidth and RTT. Less reactive to loss, better for high-bandwidth long-distance links. Used in YouTube, cloud networking.

TLS 1.3 Full Handshake (1-RTT)
Client → Server: ClientHello + key_share (ECDHE public key) + supported ciphers
Server → Client: ServerHello + key_share (server ECDHE public key)
                  + Certificate + CertificateVerify + Finished
[Both derive session keys immediately from shared ECDHE secret]
Client → Server: Finished + HTTP request
[TLS 1.2 needed 2-RTT; TLS 1.3 = 1-RTT]
0-RTT Session Resumption
Client stores session ticket from previous connection. On reconnect, sends early data in first packet — zero round trips before HTTP request. Risk: replay attacks (early data not protected against replay). Mitigate: use only for idempotent requests.
Key Improvements over TLS 1.2

Client verifies server cert chain up to trusted CA root. CT (Certificate Transparency) logs prevent mis-issuance. OCSP stapling for revocation.

Algorithms
  • Round Robin: Requests distributed evenly in rotation. Simple, ignores server load.
  • Weighted Round Robin: Servers with higher weight get more requests. For heterogeneous servers.
  • Least Connections: Route to server with fewest active connections. Better for varying request durations.
  • Least Response Time: Combines active connections + response latency.
  • IP Hash: Hash client IP → fixed server. Session stickiness (but unbalanced if some IPs dominate).

Consistent Hashing
Used for stateful routing (cache sharding, WebSocket servers).
Hash ring: servers placed on ring. Request hashed → clockwise to nearest server. Adding/removing server only remaps 1/N of keys (vs modulo hashing remaps all).

CDN Architecture
Points of Presence (PoPs): Edge servers distributed globally (Cloudflare: 300+ PoPs, Akamai: 4000+). User request routed to nearest PoP via Anycast (same IP, BGP routes to nearest datacenter) or GeoDNS.
Cache Flow
User → CDN Edge (PoP)
  → Cache HIT: return immediately (<5ms)
  → Cache MISS: fetch from origin (100-300ms), cache response, serve

Subsequent users at same PoP → cache HIT
Users at different PoP → may still be cache MISS (PoP-local cache)
Cache Control Headers
Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable     # 1 year, static assets
Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=30  # 1min fresh, serve stale while revalidating
Cache-Control: no-store                         # never cache (auth pages)
Surrogate-Control: max-age=3600                 # CDN-only hint (Varnish/Fastly)
Vary: Accept-Encoding                           # different cache per encoding

Not all content is cacheable. Edge computing (Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge) runs logic at edge. For personalized content: cache fragment (Edge Side Includes) or stream-stitch.

text: Virtual memory — paging, page tables, TLB
answer_hint:
Virtual Memory
Each process has its own virtual address space (e.g., 0 to 2^48 on 64-bit). OS maps virtual pages → physical frames via page table. Allows: isolation between processes, overcommit memory, memory-mapped files, copy-on-write.
Multi-level Page Tables
64-bit systems use 4-level (x86-64) or 5-level page tables to reduce space. Each level is a 4KB page of 512 8-byte entries. Virtual address split:
[sign ext | L4 (9) | L3 (9) | L2 (9) | L1 (9) | Offset (12)]
TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer)
Hardware cache for recent virtual→physical translations. TLB hit: 1 cycle. TLB miss: walk page table (several cycles + memory accesses). TLB flushed on context switch (unless ASID used). Huge pages (2MB/1GB) reduce TLB misses.
Page Fault
  • Minor: Page in memory but not mapped (memory-mapped file, copy-on-write) → map it
  • Major: Page not in memory → read from disk (swap). Expensive (~ms)
  • Invalid: Access to unmapped address → SIGSEGV

text: Copy-on-Write (COW) in fork() — how it works

fork() without COW
Old approach: fork duplicates entire parent address space immediately. Expensive for large processes — most forked children exec() immediately, wasting the copy.
COW Optimization
After fork(), parent and child share the same physical pages (marked read-only). On first write by either process → page fault → OS copies only that page → independent copy.
fork()
  → Page tables copied (cheap)
  → Physical pages marked read-only + copy-on-write

Child writes to variable x:
  → Page fault (read-only violation)
  → OS copies page → child gets private copy
  → Child's page marked writable
  → Parent still sees original
Where COW is used
  • fork() in Unix/Linux
  • mmap(MAP_PRIVATE): shared initially, COW on write
  • Container images: layers are shared via COW (OverlayFS)
  • Redis persistence: BGSAVE forks → COW allows snapshot without blocking writes

text: I/O models — blocking, non-blocking, I/O multiplexing, async, signals
answer_hint:
5 I/O Models
  • Blocking I/O: Thread blocks until data ready. Simple. Scales poorly (1 thread/connection).
  • Non-blocking I/O: Returns EAGAIN immediately if no data. Polling loop wastes CPU.
  • I/O Multiplexing (select/poll/epoll): One thread watches many fds. Blocks on select, wakes when any fd ready. Efficient for many connections.
  • Signal-driven I/O (SIGIO): Signal when data ready. Complex, rarely used.
  • Async I/O (AIO, io_uring): Kernel does I/O, notifies completion. True async. io_uring (Linux 5.1+): submission/completion queues in shared memory, no syscall overhead.
epoll vs select vs poll
  • select: fd_set bitmap, max 1024 fds, O(n) scan, copies fd_set each call
  • poll: array of pollfd, no 1024 limit, still O(n) scan
  • epoll: O(1) event notification. Register fds once (epoll_ctl), wait (epoll_wait) returns only ready fds. Kernel red-black tree for O(log n) add/remove. Level-triggered or edge-triggered modes.
io_uring (Modern Linux)
Fully async: app submits I/O requests to SQ ring, kernel processes, posts completions to CQ ring. Zero syscall on fast path. Used in: Tokio (Rust), QEMU, PostgreSQL, Nginx.

Coffman's Four Necessary Conditions
  • Mutual Exclusion: Resources not sharable
  • Hold and Wait: Process holds resource while waiting for another
  • No Preemption: Resources can't be forcibly taken
  • Circular Wait: T1→waits for T2→waits for T3→waits for T1
Breaking any one prevents deadlock.
Prevention
  • Eliminate Hold and Wait: Request all resources at once before starting
  • Allow Preemption: If waiting, release held resources (costly)
  • Eliminate Circular Wait: Global ordering of resources (always lock in same order)
Avoidance — Banker's Algorithm
Each process declares max resource claim. System checks if granting a request leaves system in safe state (all processes can complete). If unsafe → deny and wait. Used in theory; impractical for dynamic systems.
Detection and Recovery
Allow deadlocks to occur. Periodically run deadlock detector (wait-for graph cycle detection). Recovery: kill one victim process, or preempt + rollback resources.

text: Process scheduling — CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) in Linux
answer_hint:
CFS Algorithm
CFS maintains a virtual runtime (vruntime) per process — time the process has run, weighted by priority (nice value). Always picks the process with minimum vruntime (leftmost node in red-black tree).
vruntime Update
vruntime += actual_runtime × (NICE_0_WEIGHT / task_weight)
# Low-priority (high nice) tasks: vruntime increases faster → scheduled less
# High-priority (low nice): vruntime increases slower → scheduled more
Time Slice
No fixed time slice in CFS. Scheduling period (default 6ms) divided proportionally by weights. Minimum granularity: 0.75ms. Prevents starvation.
Priority Inheritance
When high-priority task blocks on mutex held by low-priority task → boost low-priority task's priority temporarily to prevent priority inversion (critical in RT systems).

text: Spinlock vs Mutex vs Semaphore — detailed comparison
answer_hint:
Spinlock
Thread loops (busy-waits) until lock is free. No OS involvement for uncontended case.
Pros: Near-zero overhead for very short critical sections, no context switch.
Cons: Wastes CPU if lock held long, terrible on uniprocessor, can cause priority inversion.
Use when: Critical section <~100ns (kernel code, interrupt handlers, lock-free structures).
Mutex
Thread puts itself to sleep if lock unavailable. OS wakes it when lock released.
Pros: No CPU waste while waiting, works with long critical sections.
Cons: Context switch overhead (~1-10μs), kernel involvement.
Adaptive Mutex (Linux futex): Spin briefly, then sleep. Best of both worlds.
Semaphore
Generalized mutex: can allow N concurrent holders (counting semaphore). Binary semaphore = mutex but can be released by different thread (unlike mutex, which must be released by owner). Use for: resource pools, producer-consumer signaling.
futex (Linux fast userspace mutex)
Check lock in userspace (atomic). Only make syscall when contended (wait/wake). Foundation of pthread_mutex, Java synchronized.

text: NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) — impact on performance
answer_hint:
NUMA Architecture
Multi-socket servers: each CPU socket has its own local DRAM. Accessing local memory: fast (~80ns). Accessing remote memory (other socket's DRAM): slow (~150ns, ~2x). OS/hardware provides NUMA node topology.
NUMA Problems
  • Thread on node 0 allocates, migrated to node 1 → remote memory access
  • False sharing: different threads on different NUMA nodes modify same cache line → cache coherence traffic
  • Memory-intensive apps (databases, ML) severely impacted
Mitigation
  • numactl --membind=0 --cpubind=0 ./app — bind to single NUMA node
  • numactl --interleave=all — round-robin allocation across nodes (reduces hot-spots)
  • NUMA-aware memory allocators (jemalloc, tcmalloc have NUMA support)
  • Database NUMA awareness: MySQL/PostgreSQL can bind buffer pool per node
Cache Hierarchy
L1 (4 cycles, 32KB per core) → L2 (12 cycles, 256KB per core) → L3 (30-50 cycles, shared per socket, 32-64MB) → DRAM (~200 cycles) → Remote DRAM (~400 cycles) → NVMe SSD (~100μs) → HDD (~10ms).

What is Context Switch
OS saving state of running process/thread and restoring another's. Triggered by: timer interrupt (preemption), syscall, I/O wait, voluntary yield.
Saved State

  • FPU/SIMD state (optional, lazy)
  • TLB entries (or flush TLB on switch — expensive on older hardware)
  • Process: page table base register (CR3 on x86) → TLB flush → 100s of ns extra

Cost
Process switch: ~1-100μs depending on TLB state, cache warmth, address space size. Thread switch (same process): ~1-10μs. Goroutine/coroutine switch: ~100ns (no kernel, no TLB flush — all in userspace).
Reducing Context Switches

  • Async I/O / event loops (fewer threads, less switching)
  • CPU affinity (keep thread on same core → warm L1/L2 cache)
  • Lock-free algorithms (avoid blocking)

States
CLOSED → calls go through. OPEN → calls fail-fast (no downstream). HALF_OPEN → probe call, if succeeds → CLOSED, else → OPEN.
Full Implementation
enum State { CLOSED, OPEN, HALF_OPEN }

class CircuitBreaker {
    State state = CLOSED;
    int failCount = 0, successCount = 0;
    final int failThreshold = 5;
    final int successThreshold = 2;
    Instant openedAt;
    final Duration timeout = Duration.ofSeconds(30);
    final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

    <T> T call(Supplier<T> fn) {
        lock.lock(); try {
            if (state == OPEN) {
                if (Duration.between(openedAt, Instant.now()).compareTo(timeout) > 0)
                    state = HALF_OPEN;
                else throw new CircuitOpenException();
            }
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }

        try {
            T result = fn.get();
            onSuccess(); return result;
        } catch (Exception e) { onFailure(); throw e; }
    }

    void onSuccess() {
        lock.lock(); try {
            if (state == HALF_OPEN && ++successCount >= successThreshold) {
                state = CLOSED; failCount = 0; successCount = 0;
            }
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    void onFailure() {
        lock.lock(); try {
            if (++failCount >= failThreshold || state == HALF_OPEN) {
                state = OPEN; openedAt = Instant.now(); successCount = 0;
            }
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
}

text: Design a Snowflake-style Distributed ID Generator
answer_hint:
Twitter Snowflake Structure (64-bit)
| 1 bit sign | 41 bits timestamp (ms) | 10 bits machine ID | 12 bits sequence |

- Timestamp: ms since custom epoch (Jan 1, 2010)
  → supports 2^41 ms ≈ 69 years
- Machine ID: 10 bits → 1024 machines
- Sequence: 12 bits → 4096 IDs/ms/machine

Total: ~4 million IDs/second per machine, globally unique, sortable!
Implementation
class SnowflakeIdGenerator {
    private final long EPOCH = 1288834974657L;  // Nov 4, 2010
    private final long MACHINE_ID;              // 0-1023
    private long sequence = 0;
    private long lastTs = -1;

    synchronized long nextId() {
        long ts = System.currentTimeMillis();
        if (ts == lastTs) {
            sequence = (sequence + 1) & 0xFFF;  // 12-bit mask
            if (sequence == 0) ts = waitNextMs(lastTs);  // sequence exhausted
        } else { sequence = 0; }
        lastTs = ts;
        return ((ts - EPOCH) << 22) | (MACHINE_ID << 12) | sequence;
    }

    private long waitNextMs(long ts) {
        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        while (now <= ts) now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        return now;
    }
}

What is a Bloom Filter
Space-efficient probabilistic data structure. Answers: 'definitely not in set' OR 'probably in set'. No false negatives, configurable false positive rate.
Implementation
class BloomFilter {
    private final BitSet bits;
    private final int numBits;
    private final int numHashFunctions;

    BloomFilter(int expectedItems, double falsePositiveRate) {
        // Optimal bit count: -n*ln(p) / (ln2)^2
        numBits = (int)(-expectedItems * Math.log(falsePositiveRate) / (Math.log(2)*Math.log(2)));
        // Optimal hash count: (m/n) * ln2
        numHashFunctions = (int)(numBits * 1.0 / expectedItems * Math.log(2));
        bits = new BitSet(numBits);
    }

    void add(String item) {
        for (int i = 0; i < numHashFunctions; i++)
            bits.set(Math.abs(hash(item, i)) % numBits);
    }

    boolean mightContain(String item) {
        for (int i = 0; i < numHashFunctions; i++)
            if (!bits.get(Math.abs(hash(item, i)) % numBits)) return false;  // Definitely not
        return true;  // Probably yes
    }

    private int hash(String s, int seed) {
        return Objects.hash(s, seed);
    }
}

Requirements

Core Design
class Job {
    String id; Runnable task; JobStatus status;
    long scheduledAt;  // epoch ms
    int priority, maxRetries, retryCount;
    String cronExpr;   // null for one-time jobs
}

class Scheduler {
    // Min-heap by scheduledAt
    PriorityQueue<Job> queue = new PriorityQueue<>(
        Comparator.comparingLong((Job j) -> j.scheduledAt)
                  .thenComparing(j -> -j.priority));
    ScheduledExecutorService executor = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(4);
    Map<String, ScheduledFuture<?>> running = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    String schedule(Runnable task, long delayMs, int priority) {
        Job job = new Job(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), task, 
                          System.currentTimeMillis() + delayMs, priority);
        queue.offer(job);
        return job.id;
    }

    void processJobs() {
        while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
            Job job = queue.peek();
            if (job == null || job.scheduledAt > System.currentTimeMillis()) {
                Thread.sleep(10); continue;
            }
            queue.poll();
            executor.submit(() -> executeWithRetry(job));
        }
    }

    void executeWithRetry(Job job) {
        try { job.task.run(); job.status = COMPLETED; }
        catch (Exception e) {
            if (job.retryCount++ < job.maxRetries) {
                job.scheduledAt = System.currentTimeMillis() + backoff(job.retryCount);
                queue.offer(job);
            } else { job.status = FAILED; }
        }
    }
}

    Map<String, InventoryItem> inventory = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

        try {

            if (item.availableQty < qty) return false;  // insufficient stock
            item.availableQty -= qty;
            item.reservedQty += qty;
            return true;
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    void fulfill(String productId, int qty) { // on order shipped
        // lock, reservedQty -= qty, soldQty += qty
    }

    void release(String productId, int qty) { // on order cancel
        // lock, reservedQty -= qty, availableQty += qty
    }
}

text: Design a Sliding Window Rate Limiter (code-level)
answer_hint:
Sliding Window Log Algorithm
Store timestamps of each request in a sorted set. On each request: remove old entries, count remaining, allow if below limit.
In-Memory Thread-Safe
class SlidingWindowRateLimiter {
    private final int maxRequests;
    private final long windowMs;
    private final Map<String, Deque<Long>> windows = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    boolean allow(String clientId) {
        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        long cutoff = now - windowMs;

        Deque<Long> timestamps = windows.computeIfAbsent(clientId, k -> new ArrayDeque<>());

        synchronized (timestamps) {
            // Remove expired
            while (!timestamps.isEmpty() && timestamps.peekFirst() <= cutoff)
                timestamps.pollFirst();
            if (timestamps.size() >= maxRequests) return false;
            timestamps.addLast(now);
            return true;
        }
    }
}

ZCARD rate:user1

text: Design a distributed key-value store (like Redis/DynamoDB)
answer_hint:
Architecture
Client → Load Balancer → Coordinator Node
                            ↓ (consistent hash ring)
                        Partition 0 → Replica A, B, C
                        Partition 1 → Replica D, E, F
                        ...
Data Distribution
Consistent hashing: keys mapped to ring. Each node owns a range. Virtual nodes (vnodes): each physical node = 100-200 vnodes for even distribution. Adding/removing node: only adjacent vnodes affected.
Replication
Each key replicated to N nodes (typically N=3, DynamoDB style). Coordinator writes to all N. Quorum: W=2 (write), R=2 (read) → W+R>N = strong consistency. W=1, R=1 → eventual consistency, highest availability.
Conflict Resolution
Vector clocks track causality. On divergent versions (network partition): return both to client (DynamoDB shopping cart), or last-write-wins (LWW) for simpler cases.
Storage Engine
LSM Tree (write-optimized): MemTable → immutable SSTable → compaction. B+Tree (read-optimized): InnoDB, LMDB. LSM preferred for KV stores: fast sequential writes, compaction amortizes cost.

JWT Structure
header.payload.signature

Header: {"alg": "RS256", "typ": "JWT"}
Payload: {"sub": "user123", "role": "admin", "exp": 1700000000, "iat": 1699996400}
Signature: RS256(base64url(header)+"."+base64url(payload), privateKey)

  • Content-Based: Item embeddings from metadata (genre, actors, tags). Works for new items.
  • Two-Tower Model: Separate user-tower + item-tower → embeddings → ANN search (FAISS). Pre-compute item embeddings, compute user embedding at request time. YouTube's approach.
Scoring & Ranking
Input: [user_embedding, item_embedding, context_features]
Model: Deep neural network → predicted CTR / watch_time
ANN Search: FAISS HNSW index → top-K candidates in <10ms for 100M items
A/B Testing
Split traffic by user ID hash. Primary metric: engagement (watch time, CTR). Guard metrics: don't harm diversity, churn rate. Run for statistical significance.

text: How do you detect and handle model drift?
answer_hint:
Types of Drift
  • Data drift (covariate shift): Input feature distribution changes. User behavior changed, new user segment, seasonality. Model predictions become unreliable.
  • Concept drift: Relationship between features and label changes. E.g., 'fraud' patterns evolve.
  • Label drift: Output distribution changes. E.g., more fraudulent transactions in new season.
Detection Methods
  • Statistical tests: KS-test, PSI (Population Stability Index), Chi-squared for categorical features
  • Model performance metrics: Track AUC, precision, recall on labeled samples in production
  • Shadow deployment: Run new model in shadow, compare predictions vs current model
  • Outlier detection: Flag inputs far from training distribution (z-score, isolation forest)
Response Strategy
  • Auto-retrain trigger: PSI > 0.2 → trigger retraining pipeline in MLflow/SageMaker
  • Continuous training: Retrain on rolling window of recent data (online learning for fast-moving data)
  • Canary deployment: New model serves 5% traffic, compare metrics before full rollout
Follow-ups

• How do you maintain a training data pipeline that is always fresh?

text: What is the difference between batch inference and online inference?
answer_hint:
Batch Inference
Trigger: scheduled (hourly/daily)
Input:   entire dataset (all users)
Output:  precomputed predictions stored in DB/cache
Latency: hours (acceptable)
Use cases: email recommendations, next-day demand forecast,
           weekly personalization, offline reporting

Stack: Spark/EMR → run model → write to S3 → load to serving DB
Online (Real-time) Inference
Trigger: user action (click, search, checkout)
Input:   single request features
Output:  prediction within SLA (p99 < 100ms)
Latency: milliseconds
Use cases: fraud detection, search ranking, ad bidding, chatbot

Stack: REST/gRPC → Feature store (Redis, <5ms) → Model server (TorchServe/TFServing) → Cache
Hybrid Approach
Pre-compute slow features (batch) + compute fast features (online) → merge at serving time. E.g., Netflix: batch compute user long-term embeddings + online compute session context → real-time ranking.
Follow-ups
• How do you optimize model inference latency? (quantization, ONNX runtime, model pruning)
• What is model serving and how does TorchServe handle batching?

Core Components
Experiment Config Service → stores experiment definition
  (variants, allocation %, targeting rules, metrics)

Assignment Service → deterministic bucketing by user_id
  hash(user_id + experiment_id) % 100 < allocation%
  → same user always in same bucket (sticky assignment)
  → results cached in Redis

Event Tracking → user actions logged with experiment_id + variant
  → Kafka → Data Warehouse (Clickhouse/BigQuery)

Analysis Service → daily/real-time stats computation
  → t-test / z-test for significance
  → dashboard with p-value, confidence interval, lift %
Statistical Concepts
  • p-value < 0.05: Less than 5% chance result is due to random variation
  • Statistical power: Probability of detecting a real effect. Usually target 80%.
  • MDE (Minimum Detectable Effect): Smallest effect worth detecting → determines sample size
  • Sample size calculator: n = 16σ²/δ² (for 80% power, 5% significance)
  • Multiple testing problem: 20 experiments at 5% significance → 1 false positive on average. Fix: Bonferroni correction or FDR.
Common Pitfalls
  • Novelty effect: New feature gets engagement just because it's new — run longer
  • Network effect: Treating control and treatment users who interact with each other — cluster randomization
  • Peeking: Stopping early when p < 0.05 inflates false positive rate — use sequential testing

text: How does a fraud detection system work?
answer_hint:
Layered Defense Architecture
Transaction Request
    ↓ (sync, <200ms)
1. Rules Engine (hard rules, fast)
   - Deny if: card stolen (blocklist), impossible geography, country blocked
   - Flag if: unusual amount, new device
    ↓
2. ML Model (gradient boosting / neural net, <50ms)
   - Features: velocity (5 txns in 1min), device fingerprint, merchant category,
               user history embedding, IP reputation, network graph features
   - Output: fraud probability score 0-1
    ↓
3. Decision: score < 0.3 → approve | 0.3-0.7 → 3DS challenge | > 0.7 → decline
    ↓ (async, post-transaction)
4. Chargeback feedback → retrain loop
Key Features
  • Velocity features: count(txns) per user/card/device in last 1m/5m/1h/24h using Redis sliding window
  • Device fingerprinting: browser/app fingerprint, cookie, canvas fingerprint
  • Network graph: card linked to account linked to device → graph neural network for collusion
  • Geospatial: impossible travel (transaction in Mumbai then London in 30min)
Class Imbalance
Fraud rate: 0.1-1%. Training: oversample fraud (SMOTE), undersample legitimate, or use class weights. Evaluation metric: precision@threshold, recall, AUC-ROC. NOT accuracy (99% accuracy by saying everything is legitimate).
Follow-ups

text: Explain transformer architecture and attention mechanism
answer_hint:
Self-Attention Mechanism
Input: sequence of tokens → embeddings (d_model=768 for BERT-base)

For each token, compute:
  Q (query) = embedding × W_Q
  K (key)   = embedding × W_K
  V (value) = embedding × W_V

Attention weights = softmax(Q × K^T / sqrt(d_k))
Output = Attention_weights × V

# Each token attends to all other tokens — captures long-range dependencies
# Multi-head: run h parallel attention heads, concat, project
Transformer Architecture
  • Encoder (BERT): Bidirectional. Sees full context. Used for classification, NER, embeddings.
  • Decoder (GPT): Autoregressive. Each token attends only to previous tokens (causal mask). Used for generation.
  • Encoder-Decoder (T5, BART): Seq2seq tasks: translation, summarization, QA.
Why Transformers replaced RNNs
  • RNN: sequential computation → no parallelism. Gradient vanishing for long sequences.
  • Transformer: parallel over all positions. Self-attention = O(n²d) but parallelizable on GPU.
  • Position encoding: sinusoidal or learned — since attention is permutation-invariant, positional info must be added explicitly.
Follow-ups

Search Stack
User Query
    ↓
Query Understanding: spell check, tokenization, synonym expansion, intent classification
    ↓
Retrieval (Elasticsearch / Lucene):
  BM25 score: TF-IDF with length normalization
  → top-1000 candidates in <50ms
    ↓
Learning-to-Rank (LTR) Model:
  Features: BM25 score, query-doc semantic similarity,
            user click history, item popularity, freshness, location
  Model: LightGBM / BERT cross-encoder
  → rerank top-1000 to top-10
    ↓
Business Rules: boost paid listings, filter unavailable items
    ↓ 
Response
Elasticsearch Internals
  • Inverted index: term → [doc_id, positions]. Builds at index time.
  • Sharding: index split into shards. Search parallelized across shards.
  • Analyzers: tokenizer + filters (lowercase, stemming, stopwords) at index + query time
  • Boosting: title^3 body^1 — title matches worth 3x body matches
Learning-to-Rank
  • Pointwise: Independent regression/classification per document
  • Pairwise (RankNet): Prefer doc A over B → binary classification
  • Listwise (LambdaMART): Optimize NDCG directly. Best quality.

text: How do you diagnose and fix high API latency?
answer_hint:
Systematic Approach
1. MEASURE: Where is the time going?
   - Add distributed tracing (Jaeger/Zipkin): see each span's duration
   - p50/p95/p99 latency (NOT just average — outliers matter)
   - Breakdown: network + serialization + DB queries + external API + CPU

2. IDENTIFY bottleneck:
   Common causes:
   - N+1 queries (add JOIN FETCH or batch)
   - Missing DB index (check EXPLAIN ANALYZE → seq scan)
   - Synchronous external API call in critical path (make async / cache)
   - Lock contention (connection pool exhausted, mutex hotspot)
   - GC pauses (Java: -XX:+PrintGCDetails, G1/ZGC tuning)
   - Memory pressure (swap, cache thrashing)

3. FIX:
   - Caching: Redis in front of slow DB queries
   - Async: move non-critical work off request path (Kafka)
   - Parallelism: concurrent DB queries (CompletableFuture/goroutines)
   - Index: add composite index for slow query
   - Connection pooling: tune min/max pool size
Key Metrics
  • Latency percentiles: p50=100ms is fine; p99=5s means 1% users wait 5 seconds
  • Throughput: RPS the service can handle without degrading
  • Error rate: 5xx rate as % of total requests
  • Saturation: CPU%, memory%, connection pool utilization, queue depth
USE Method
For every resource: Utilization (how busy), Saturation (how much queuing), Errors (error count). Invented by Brendan Gregg.
Follow-ups
• How do you use flame graphs to identify CPU hotspots?
• What is the difference between tail latency and average latency?
• How do you implement circuit breakers to protect against latency cascades?

text: Explain distributed tracing — how it works
answer_hint:
How it works
Request enters Service A → Tracer generates trace_id (128-bit)
Service A calls Service B → propagates trace_id + span_id in HTTP header:
  traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
               version  traceId                    parentSpanId   flags

Each service creates a span:
  span = {traceId, spanId, parentSpanId, name, startTime, duration,
          tags: {"db.type":"postgresql", "http.status":200},
          logs: [{"event":"query", "sql":"..."}]}

Spans sent async to collector (Jaeger/Zipkin) → assembled into trace tree
OpenTelemetry (OTel)
  • Vendor-neutral standard for traces, metrics, logs
  • SDK instruments your code (auto-instrumentation for popular frameworks)
  • Exporter sends to Jaeger, Zipkin, Tempo, AWS X-Ray, Datadog
  • OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=jaeger OTEL_EXPORTER_JAEGER_ENDPOINT=http://jaeger:14268/api/traces
Sampling
  • Head sampling: Decision at trace start (before outcome known). Simple. Loses tail errors.
  • Tail sampling: Buffer traces, decide after seeing all spans. Can keep errored/slow traces.
  • Rate: 1% for healthy services, 100% for errors, 10% for slow (p99 > 1s)
Follow-ups

• How do you correlate traces with logs and metrics? (structured logging with trace_id)

text: Cache strategies — cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-back
answer_hint:
Cache Strategies
  • Cache-Aside (Lazy loading): App checks cache first; on miss, reads DB, populates cache. Cache only stores what's actually requested. Risk: thundering herd on cold start.
  • Read-Through: Cache reads from DB automatically on miss (library handles it). App always reads from cache. DB not directly accessed by app.
  • Write-Through: Write to cache AND DB synchronously. Cache never stale. High write latency (must wait for both). Good for read-heavy.
  • Write-Back (Write-Behind): Write to cache, return immediately. Write to DB asynchronously. Fast writes. Risk: data loss if cache crashes before flush.
Cache-Aside Pattern (most common)
def get_user(user_id):
    # Try cache first
    user = redis.get(f"user:{user_id}")
    if user:
        return deserialize(user)  # cache hit
    
    # Cache miss — read from DB
    user = db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=%s", user_id)
    
    # Populate cache with TTL
    redis.setex(f"user:{user_id}", ttl=3600, value=serialize(user))
    return user

def update_user(user_id, data):
    db.execute("UPDATE users SET ... WHERE id=%s", user_id)
    redis.delete(f"user:{user_id}")  # invalidate — don't update!
Cache Eviction Policies
  • LRU: Evict least recently used. Good general-purpose.
  • LFU: Evict least frequently used. Better for skewed access patterns.
  • TTL: Time-based expiry. Always stale by at most TTL seconds.
  • Allkeys-lru (Redis): Apply LRU across all keys when memory full.
Follow-ups
• What is the thundering herd problem and how do you prevent it? (mutex/lock on cache miss, staggered TTLs)
• How do you handle cache warming after a cold restart?
• What is probabilistic early expiration (PER) and how does it prevent dogpile?

text: Load testing — how to approach and what tools to use
answer_hint:
Test Types
  • Load test: Expected normal + peak load. Validate SLAs. Measure p99 latency, throughput, error rate.
  • Stress test: Push beyond expected load until system breaks. Find breaking point. Test recovery.
  • Soak/endurance test: Normal load for extended time (hours/days). Find memory leaks, connection exhaustion, log rotation issues.
  • Spike test: Sudden large traffic burst. Test autoscaling, circuit breakers.
  • Chaos test: Kill instances, inject latency, corrupt network. Test resilience.
k6 Example
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  stages: [
    { duration: '2m', target: 100 },   // ramp up to 100 VUs
    { duration: '5m', target: 100 },   // hold at 100 VUs
    { duration: '2m', target: 0 },     // ramp down
  ],
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration': ['p(99)<500'],  // 99% requests < 500ms
    'http_req_failed': ['rate<0.01'],   // <1% error rate
  },
};

export default function() {
  const r = http.get('https://api.example.com/users');
  check(r, { 'status 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(1);
}

  • Latency: p50, p95, p99, p999 as load increases

  • Resource utilization: CPU, memory, disk I/O, network on each tier

text: Observability — metrics, logs, traces — the three pillars
answer_hint:
Three Pillars
  • Metrics: Numeric aggregations over time. Low cardinality. Cheap to store. Tool: Prometheus (pull-based scraping) + Grafana. Counter, Gauge, Histogram, Summary.
  • Logs: Discrete events with context. High volume. Searchable. Tool: ELK stack (Elasticsearch+Logstash+Kibana) or Loki+Grafana. Structured JSON logs with trace_id for correlation.
  • Traces: Request journey across services. Tool: Jaeger, Zipkin, Tempo. Essential for microservices debugging.
SLI / SLO / SLA / Error Budget
SLI (Service Level Indicator): the metric you measure
  e.g., "% of requests with latency < 200ms"

SLO (Service Level Objective): your internal target
  e.g., "99.9% of requests < 200ms over rolling 30 days"

SLA (Service Level Agreement): contractual with customer
  e.g., "99.5% uptime or credit applied"

Error Budget: 1 - SLO = allowed unreliability
  99.9% SLO = 0.1% error budget = 43.8 min downtime/month
  If budget exhausted: freeze feature work, focus on reliability
RED Method (for services)
Rate (requests/sec), Error rate (errors/sec), Duration (latency). Apply to every microservice for quick health check.

text: How does CPU caching work and why does it matter for performance?
answer_hint:
Memory Hierarchy
L1 cache:  ~32KB per core,   ~1ns  latency
L2 cache: ~256KB per core,   ~4ns  latency
L3 cache:   ~8MB shared,     ~40ns latency
RAM:        ~16-64GB,       ~100ns latency
SSD NVMe:              ~100μs latency
HDD:                    ~10ms latency
Cache Lines
Data loaded in 64-byte cache lines. Accessing one byte loads entire 64-byte block. Sequential access (arrays) → excellent cache utilization. Random access (linked lists) → cache miss per node.
False Sharing
# Two threads update different variables in same cache line:
# Thread 1 updates counter_a, Thread 2 updates counter_b
# If they're adjacent in memory → same cache line → cache coherence traffic
# Core 1 invalidates Core 2's cache line on every write → performance degrades!

# Fix: padding
struct PaddedCounter {
    alignas(64) std::atomic<int64_t> value;  // 64-byte aligned
    char padding[64 - sizeof(std::atomic<int64_t>)];  // fill rest of cache line
};
Practical Impact
  • Array of structs vs Struct of arrays (SOA): SOA = better cache usage for column-wise processing
  • Cache-oblivious algorithms (recursive divide) beat sequential for large matrices
  • Go: sync.Mutex padded to avoid false sharing with adjacent data
